title: Anticipatory vibrotactile cueing facilitates grip force adjustment
research_question: How do anticipatory vibrotactile cues influence the latency and magnitude of grip force adjustment in response to an unexpected load disturbance?

participants.description: Five volunteer participants (excluding authors) from the research staff of the institution, wore headphones playing pink noise.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: An instrumented and actuated parallelepiped-shaped handle held between the thumb and index finger. The handle could be jerked (pulling force) and/or provide vibrotactile stimulation (250 Hz or 100 Hz) to the gripping fingers. Four main conditions: 1) Load only, 2) Vibrotactile only (250 Hz), 3) Load + Vibrotactile (250 Hz, 50 ms before load), 4) Load + Vibrotactile (100 Hz, 50 ms before load). A follow-up Condition 5 (Vibrotactile only) was used for conscious response.

measures.instrument: Time difference between onset of traction force/vibrotactile cue end and onset of grip force change (threshold 20 N/s)
Difference between maximum grip force and average of 100 ms before onset of traction/vibrotactile stimulation
Difference between highest position after force stimulus and average of 100 ms before onset of traction, measured by encoder
Differential acceleration between nail and contact surface, integrated twice
High resolution, high bandwidth force sensor (Kistler 9217A)

findings.mechanism: Grip force and finger mechanics depend on individual tissue properties and neural responses.
findings.quote: P2's grip-force increases were the lowest but the finger deformation was the largest among the participants. P3's grip-force increases were greatest but the finger skin deformations were lowest.

mechanisms: Vibrotactile stimulation provides early-warning signals to the nervous system, influencing reflex actions rather than conscious responses.
Initial dynamics of finger-object interaction are dominated by tissue mechanics, followed by neural responses that vary individually.
moderators: Individual differences in biomechanical properties and neural responses
implementation_implications: Anticipatory vibrotactile cues can shorten the latency of grip force adjustment, which could be useful for robotic and rehabilitation purposes to achieve more stable human grasp.

tables.description: Averages and standard deviations of latency, grip increase, and grip handle displacement across five conditions (load only, vib only, load+vib 250Hz, load+vib 100Hz, vib only conscious).

limitations: Small sample size (N=5) limits generalizability of individual differences.
Frequency tuning method for vibrotactile stimulation does not always ensure activation of specific receptor classes.
Drawing conclusions from apparent correlations between grip force and finger deformation is risky due to complex biomechanics and neural responses.

mechanism_chain.description: Vibrotactile cues provide anticipatory information about upcoming load changes, allowing the motor system to pre-program or adjust grip force proactively, leading to faster and more stable grip force responses.

steps.to_construct: Pre-programmed motor command for grip force adjustment
